claims.text: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys under low-field cycling are governed primarily by crystallographic order and grain-boundary density rather than solely by composition.
Increasing grain-boundary density and reducing long-range order broadens the magnetostructural transition.
Increasing grain-boundary density and reducing long-range order reduces hysteresis.
Increasing grain-boundary density and reducing long-range order produces a more gradual and less sharply peaked entropy change.
The as-deposited films or foils have a mixed or partially ordered hexagonal phase and high defect density.
Annealing at 400–600°C for 1–4 hours promotes partial ordering and grain growth relative to the as-deposited state.
Grain boundaries and disorder act as nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Grain boundaries and disorder act as barriers to the magnetostructural transition.
Grain boundaries and disorder reduce the energy barrier for phase change.
A reduced phase-change energy barrier decreases hysteresis and spreads the entropy change over a wider temperature range.
Annealed samples with lower grain-boundary density and higher order will show a sharper and more hysteretic magnetocaloric response.
As-deposited samples with high grain-boundary density and disorder will show a broader, less hysteretic, and more gradual entropy-change profile.
The as-deposited microstructural state improves heat-exchange rates and reduces losses.
The prediction is limited to non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films or foils under low-field cycling and moderate annealing and may not apply to bulk ingots or equiatomic compositions.
Most prior studies concern bulk or melt-spun materials rather than as-deposited thin films.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says controlled annealing can increase grain-boundary density and reduce long-range order, whereas the specified annealing intervention is said to cause grain growth and increased partial ordering, which would generally lower grain-boundary density and increase order.

Grain boundaries and disorder are described both as barriers to the transition and as features that reduce the phase-change energy barrier; the distinction between kinetic obstruction and nucleation-barrier reduction is not explained.
